source_batch.unit_label: Module B unit 3 (part 1): Risk Regulations in Banking Industry - Basel I, II and III history

facts.statement: Banking is regulated because a healthy banking system underpins the economy, banks lend depositors' money in a highly leveraged business, and mismanaged risk-taking can cause disastrous failures; the regulator in India is the Reserve Bank. The goals of regulation are: improving the safety of the banking industry by imposing capital requirements in line with banks' risks (the risk-based capital or capital adequacy principle); levelling the competitive playing field through common benchmarks; promoting sound business and supervisory practices; controlling and monitoring systemic risk; and protecting depositors, who cannot impose real market discipline on banks. Systemic risk is the risk of failure of the whole banking system, since the failure of one bank can spread through mutual lending, borrowing and other commitments; combining deposit insurance with capital regulation is needed because deposit insurance encourages banks to reduce equity capital.

The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), started in 1930, is owned by central banks of different countries including India, serves as a bank for member central banks and fosters international monetary and financial stability, and is based in Basel. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) was established by the central bank governors of the Group of Ten countries at the end of 1974 after serious disturbances in international currency and banking markets, notably the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt in West Germany on 26 June 1974, which created the settlement risk from time-zone differences known as Herstatt risk. The Committee's headquarters are at the BIS in Basel, it has no formal supranational supervisory authority and its standards are not legally binding but are recommendations for national implementation. It issued the Concordat in 1975 (revised in 1983) on sharing supervisory responsibility for banks' foreign establishments, and the Core Principles for effective banking supervision in 1997 (25 principles, now 29 after revision in September 2012).

The 1988 Basel Accord (Basel I) set minimum capital requirements for banks linked to credit exposure: a minimum ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets of 8 per cent, implemented by the end of 1992 in the G-10 countries. Assets were grouped into five risk weights (0, 10, 20, 50 and 100 per cent): government debt generally at 0 per cent, bank debt at 20 per cent, residential mortgages at 50 per cent and other debt at 100 per cent; off-balance sheet items such as performance guarantees and letters of credit were brought in through credit conversion factors. Capital had Tier 1 (equity and disclosed reserves) and Tier 2 (undisclosed reserves, revaluation reserves, general provisions and loan-loss reserves, hybrid and subordinated debt). The capital to risk-weighted assets ratio is called the Cooke ratio; in India it is the CRAR.

The 1996 amendment to the Basel Accord, brought into effect in 1998, added an explicit capital cushion for market risk in trading activities. It allowed banks to use proprietary value at risk models: VaR computed daily at the 99th percentile, one-tailed, over a ten trading day horizon using at least one year of historical observation; the capital charge is the higher of the previous day's VaR and three times the average daily VaR of the preceding 60 business days; back testing sets a plus factor added to the multiplier of three; banks may issue short-term subordinated debt with a lock-in (Tier 3) to meet part of market risk capital; an alternative standardised building block approach calculates general and specific market risk separately; banks must segregate the trading book and mark it to market.

Basel I was revised because credit risk weights were not risk-sensitive enough (all corporates at 100 per cent whether rated AAA or B, all banks at 20 per cent), it encouraged decisions driven by regulatory constraints rather than economics, it did not recognise credit risk mitigants such as credit derivatives, securitisation, collateral and guarantees, and it did not cover operational risk. Basel II (published June 2004, with a comprehensive version in June 2006) rests on three pillars: minimum capital requirements, supervisory review of capital adequacy and internal assessment, and market discipline through disclosure. Pillar 1 approaches in increasing sophistication: for credit risk, the standardised approach and the foundation and advanced internal ratings based approaches; for market risk, the standardised approach (maturity method or duration method) and internal models; for operational risk, the basic indicator, standardised and advanced measurement approaches. Pillar 2 covers risk assessment, soundness of internal processes, maintenance of minimum capital with prompt corrective action for shortfall and differential capital where processes are weak; Pillar 3 covers enhanced disclosure.

Basel III was the response to the 2008 financial crisis, in which banks had too much leverage and inadequate liquidity buffers, poor governance and risk management and weak incentive structures; the Basel Committee issued Principles for sound liquidity risk management and supervision in September 2008 and Basel III standards in December 2010, endorsed by the G20 at Seoul in November 2010. Its innovations: a higher quality and quantity of capital; a capital conservation buffer of common equity that restricts pay-outs when breached; a countercyclical capital buffer restricting participation in system-wide credit booms; a leverage ratio as a backstop to risk-based capital; liquidity standards (the Liquidity Coverage Ratio for 30 days of stress, phased from 60 per cent in 2015 to 100 per cent in 2019, and the Net Stable Funding Ratio, a minimum standard from 1 January 2018); and supplementary requirements for systemically important banks. Basel III kept three pillars, enhanced as minimum capital and liquidity requirements, supervisory review with firm-wide risk management and capital planning, and enhanced disclosure. The BCBS minimum common equity and Tier 1 ratios were 4.5 per cent and 6 per cent from 2015.

Under the Reserve Bank's Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025 a bank maintains a minimum total capital of 9 per cent of risk-weighted assets (CRAR) on an ongoing basis; CET1 at least 5.5 per cent; Tier 1 at least 7 per cent (so AT1 admitted at most 1.5 per cent); Tier 2 at most 2 per cent within the 9 per cent; and, in addition, a capital conservation buffer of 2.5 per cent in the form of CET1. The minimum CET1 plus the buffer is therefore 8 per cent and the minimum total capital plus the buffer is 11.5 per cent. A wholly owned subsidiary of a foreign bank maintains a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 10 per cent for an initial three years from commencement, plus the buffers. Capital adequacy is assessed at solo and consolidated (group) levels; insurance and non-financial subsidiaries are not consolidated. The courseware adds that Basel III capital regulation took effect in India from 1 April 2013 in phases; the last tranche of the capital conservation buffer (0.625 per cent) was deferred by a circular of 5 February 2021 from 1 April 2021 to 1 October 2021, so the minimum buffer was 1.875 per cent and the minimum CRAR 10.875 per cent until 30 September 2021, and from 1 October 2021 the full 2.5 per cent and 11.5 per cent.
facts.locator: Paragraphs 7, 11 and Table 1; S03 printed pp. 324-325, sections 13.7.1 and 13.7.2

facts.statement: Under the Directions a bank computes capital for operational risk under the Basic Indicator Approach: capital equal to the average over the previous three years of 15 per cent (alpha) of positive annual gross income, excluding years with zero or negative gross income from numerator and denominator. The market risk capital charge is the sum of the capital requirements for interest rate risk, equity risk and foreign exchange risk, and risk weighted assets for market risk are the capital charge multiplied by 12.5. The courseware says that in 2007 the Reserve Bank decided that commercial banks should adopt the standardised approach for credit risk, the Basic Indicator Approach for operational risk by March 2009 and the standardised duration approach for market risk, with advanced approaches possible only with the Reserve Bank's prior approval.
facts.locator: Paragraphs 185 and 214 to 215; S03 printed p. 325, section 13.7.2

payload.title: Why banks are regulated and what regulation aims to do
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Why**: banking is the **backbone of the economy**; banks lend **depositors' money** in a **highly leveraged** business; unregulated risk-taking can produce **disastrous failures**. In India the regulator is the **Reserve Bank**.

**Goals of regulation**
1. **Safety**: capital in line with risk (**risk-based capital / capital adequacy**).
2. **Level playing field**: **common benchmarks** for all banks.
3. **Sound business and supervisory practice**.
4. **Control of systemic risk**.
5. **Protect depositors**, who **cannot impose real market discipline** on banks.

**Systemic risk** = failure of the **whole system**. One bank's failure spreads through **mutual lending, borrowing and commitments**. **Deposit insurance** alone is not enough because it **encourages banks to shrink equity**, so it is **combined with capital rules**.

payload.title: The BIS and the Basel Committee
payload.core_explanation_md:
**BIS**: started **1930**, **owned by central banks** (India's included), **a bank for central banks**, fosters **monetary and financial stability**, **based in Basel**.

**BCBS**: set up **end-1974** by the **G-10 central bank governors** after the **failure of Bankhaus Herstatt (26 June 1974)**, which showed **settlement risk from time-zone gaps** (**Herstatt risk**). Its **headquarters** are at the **BIS in Basel**.

- **No legal force**: it has **no supranational supervisory authority**; its standards are **recommendations** that national authorities implement.
- **Concordat**: **1975**, revised **1983**, on sharing supervision of banks' **foreign establishments**.
- **Core Principles for effective banking supervision**: **1997**, **25 principles**; **29** after the **September 2012** revision.

payload.title: Basel I: the 8% accord and the risk weight buckets
payload.core_explanation_md:
**1988 Accord**: **minimum capital to risk-weighted assets of 8%**, in force in the G-10 by **end-1992**.

| Risk weight | Typical assets |
| --- | --- |
| **0%** | **government debt** |
| **10%, 20%** | **bank debt (20%)** |
| **50%** | **residential mortgages** |
| **100%** | **other debt, corporates** |

**Off-balance sheet items** (performance guarantees, letters of credit) enter through **credit conversion factors**.

**Capital**: **Tier 1** = **equity and disclosed reserves**; **Tier 2** = **undisclosed reserves, revaluation reserves, general provisions and loan-loss reserves, hybrid and subordinated debt**.

**Cooke ratio** = **capital ÷ risk-weighted assets** (**CRAR** in India).

payload.title: The 1996 amendment: capital for market risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
Added in **1996**, effective **1998**, to cover **price risk in trading**.

- Banks may use **their own value at risk (VaR) models**: **daily VaR**, **99th percentile, one-tailed**, **10 trading days**, **at least one year of history**.
- **Capital charge** = the **higher of** **yesterday's VaR** and **3 × the average daily VaR of the last 60 business days**.
- **Back testing** sets a **plus factor** added to the multiplier of **3**.
- **Tier 3**: **short-term subordinated debt with a lock-in** may meet part of market risk capital.
- **Standardised alternative**: the **building block** approach (**general** and **specific** market risk **added up**).
- Banks must **separate the trading book** and **mark it to market**.

payload.title: Why Basel I was revised, and Basel II's three pillars
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Basel I's weaknesses**: weights **not risk-sensitive** (all corporates at 100%, **AAA same as B**; all banks at 20%); **regulation-driven decisions** rather than economic ones; **no credit for mitigants** (derivatives, securitisation, collateral, guarantees); **no operational risk**.

**Basel II** (**June 2004**, comprehensive version **June 2006**)
| Pillar | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **1 Minimum capital** | credit, market and **new** operational risk |
| **2 Supervisory review** | assess risk, **soundness of internal processes**, **minimum capital with prompt corrective action**, **extra capital** where processes are weak |
| **3 Market discipline** | **enhanced disclosure** (core and supplementary, timely) |

payload.title: The Pillar 1 menu of approaches
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Risk | Approaches, **simplest to most advanced** |
| --- | --- |
| **Credit** | **Standardised**; **Foundation IRB**; **Advanced IRB** |
| **Market** | **Standardised** (**maturity method** or **duration method**); **internal models** |
| **Operational** | **Basic Indicator**; **Standardised**; **Advanced Measurement** |

More advanced approaches are **more risk-sensitive** and need **supervisory approval**.

payload.title: Basel III: why, and what it added
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Why**: the **2008 crisis** exposed **too much leverage**, **thin liquidity buffers**, **weak governance and incentives**. BCBS issued **liquidity principles (September 2008)** and **Basel III (December 2010)**, endorsed by the **G20 at Seoul (November 2010)**.

**Innovations**
- **Better and more capital**: BCBS minimum **common equity 4.5%** and **Tier 1 6%** from **2015**.
- **Capital conservation buffer**: **common equity**; if breached, **pay-outs are restricted**.
- **Countercyclical buffer**: curbs **bank participation in system-wide credit booms**.
- **Leverage ratio**: **backstop** to risk-based capital.
- **LCR**: **30 days of stress**, **60% in 2015 to 100% in 2019**.
- **NSFR**: **minimum standard from 1 January 2018** (longer-term funding mismatch).
- **Systemically important banks**: **extra requirements**.

**Three pillars kept**, each **enhanced**.

payload.title: Indian minimum capital ratios under Basel III
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Item | % of risk-weighted assets |
| --- | --- |
| **Minimum CET1** | **5.5** |
| **Minimum Tier 1** | **7.0** (so **AT1 at most 1.5**) |
| **Minimum total capital (CRAR)** | **9.0** (so **Tier 2 at most 2.0**) |
| **Capital conservation buffer (CET1)** | **2.5** |
| **CET1 + buffer** | **8.0** |
| **Total capital + buffer** | **11.5** |

- **Foreign bank wholly owned subsidiary**: **10%** minimum for the **first three years**, plus buffers.
- **Levels**: **solo** and **consolidated**; **insurance and non-financial subsidiaries are not consolidated**.
- **Phasing (courseware)**: from **1 April 2013**; the **last 0.625% of the buffer** was **deferred to 1 October 2021**, so until **30 September 2021** buffer **1.875%** and CRAR **10.875%**; from **1 October 2021** **2.5%** and **11.5%**.

payload.title: How the Directions build capital for operational and market risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Operational risk: Basic Indicator Approach**: capital = **average over the previous three years of 15% (alpha) of positive annual gross income**; **years with zero or negative gross income are left out** of both numerator and denominator.

**Market risk**: charge = **interest rate risk + equity risk + foreign exchange risk**; **risk weighted assets for market risk = charge × 12.5**.

**History (courseware)**: in **2007** the Reserve Bank asked banks to adopt the **standardised approach** (credit), **Basic Indicator** (operational, by **March 2009**) and the **standardised duration approach** (market); **advanced approaches** need **prior RBI approval**.

payload.title: The capital charge for market risk under the 1996 amendment
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank using its own model has a previous day's ten-day VaR of ₹12 crore and an average daily VaR over the preceding 60 business days of ₹9 crore, with the multiplier at 3. What is the market risk capital charge, and what if the previous day's VaR had been ₹30 crore?

worked_steps.description: Compare with the previous day's VaR of 12.
If the previous day's VaR were ₹30 crore.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The charge is ₹27 crore; it would be ₹30 crore if the previous day's VaR were ₹30 crore

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the charge the higher of the two figures?
self_check.expected_takeaway: So that a sudden rise in risk (a high previous day VaR) is capitalised at once, while the multiple of the 60-day average guards against understating risk in calm periods.

payload.title: Risk-weighted assets and the capital ratio under Basel I weights
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank holds government securities of ₹200 crore (0% weight), claims on banks of ₹300 crore (20%), residential mortgage loans of ₹400 crore (50%) and corporate loans of ₹500 crore (100%). Find its risk-weighted assets, the capital needed at 8% and at 9%, and its ratio if it holds capital of ₹95 crore.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: Risk-weighted assets are ₹760 crore; capital needed is ₹60.8 crore at 8% and ₹68.4 crore at 9%; a bank with ₹95 crore has a 12.5% ratio

self_check.prompt_text: Why do the government securities add nothing to the risk-weighted assets?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They carry a 0% risk weight, so they need no capital for credit risk.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is a goal of banking regulation?

options.text_md: Protecting depositors, who cannot impose real market discipline on banks

payload.correct_explanation_md: Regulation aims to improve safety through capital requirements, level the playing field, promote sound practices, control systemic risk and protect depositors.

payload.stem_md: What is systemic risk?

options.text_md: The risk of one borrower defaulting
The risk of exchange rate movement
The risk of failure of the whole banking system, which one bank's failure can trigger through interconnections
The risk of system software failure

payload.correct_explanation_md: Systemic risk is the risk of failure of the whole banking system; one bank's failure can spread through mutual lending, borrowing and commitments.

payload.stem_md: Why is deposit insurance combined with capital regulation?

options.text_md: Because deposit insurance encourages banks to reduce equity capital to improve returns

payload.correct_explanation_md: Deposit insurance can encourage banks to reduce equity capital, so it needs to be combined with regulation on the capital banks must hold.

payload.stem_md: In what year was the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision established, and by whom?

options.text_md: At the end of 1974, by the central bank governors of the Group of Ten countries

payload.correct_explanation_md: The Basel Committee was established by the G-10 central bank governors at the end of 1974.

payload.stem_md: The failure of which bank in 1974 prompted the creation of the Basel Committee?

options.text_md: Bank of Credit and Commerce International

payload.correct_explanation_md: The Herstatt incident of 26 June 1974 prompted the G-10 countries to form the Committee.

payload.stem_md: What is the legal force of the Basel Committee's standards?

options.text_md: None of its own; they are recommendations that national authorities implement in their own systems

payload.correct_explanation_md: The Committee has no formal supranational supervisory authority; its conclusions are recommendations of best practice for national implementation.

payload.stem_md: What minimum ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets did the 1988 Accord set?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The 1988 Accord called for a minimum capital to risk-weighted assets ratio of 8 per cent by the end of 1992.

payload.stem_md: Under the 1988 Accord which risk weight applied generally to bank debt?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Government debt was generally at 0 per cent, bank debt at 20 per cent, residential mortgages at 50 per cent and other debt at 100 per cent.

payload.stem_md: What is the Cooke ratio?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The Cooke ratio is capital to risk-weighted assets, the CRAR in India.

payload.stem_md: Under the 1996 amendment, how is the capital charge for a bank using its own VaR model determined?

options.text_md: The higher of the previous day's VaR and three times the average daily VaR of the preceding 60 business days
Three times the previous day's VaR

payload.correct_explanation_md: The capital charge is the higher of the previous day's VaR and three times the average daily VaR of the preceding 60 business days.

payload.stem_md: Which confidence level and horizon does the 1996 amendment prescribe for VaR?

options.text_md: 99th percentile one-tailed, over ten trading days

payload.correct_explanation_md: VaR is computed daily at the 99th percentile, one-tailed, over a time horizon of ten trading days.

payload.stem_md: What is Tier 3 capital in the 1996 amendment?

options.text_md: Short-term subordinated debt subject to a lock-in clause, to meet part of market risk

payload.correct_explanation_md: Banks may issue short-term subordinated debt subject to a lock-in clause (Tier 3) to meet a part of their market risks.

payload.stem_md: Which was a criticism of Basel I that led to its revision?

options.text_md: It treated an AAA corporate and a B rated corporate alike at 100 per cent
It covered operational risk too heavily

payload.correct_explanation_md: Basel I applied uniform risk weights, so an AAA and a B rated company were treated identically.

payload.stem_md: What are the three pillars of Basel II?

options.explanation_md: These are the risks in Pillar 1.

options.text_md: Minimum capital requirements, supervisory review, and market discipline

payload.correct_explanation_md: Basel II rests on minimum capital requirements, supervisory review of capital adequacy and internal assessment, and market discipline through disclosure.

payload.stem_md: Which is NOT an approach for operational risk capital in Basel II?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Operational risk approaches are the basic indicator, standardised and advanced measurement approaches; the IRB approaches are for credit risk.

payload.stem_md: What does Pillar 2 of Basel II include?

options.text_md: Evaluating banks' risk assessment and ensuring minimum capital, with prompt corrective action for shortfall

payload.correct_explanation_md: Pillar 2 covers risk assessment, soundness of internal processes, maintenance of minimum capital with prompt corrective action and differential capital where processes are slack.

payload.stem_md: Which event prompted the move towards Basel III?

options.text_md: The 2008 financial crisis and the failure of Lehman Brothers

payload.correct_explanation_md: The crisis, with excess leverage and inadequate liquidity buffers, led to Basel III standards issued in December 2010.

payload.stem_md: Which of these was NOT introduced by Basel III?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Basel III introduced a conservation buffer, countercyclical buffer, leverage ratio, LCR and NSFR; the market risk amendment dates from 1996.

payload.stem_md: What does the Liquidity Coverage Ratio ensure?

options.text_md: Enough high quality liquid assets to meet cash outflows over a 30-day period of stress

payload.correct_explanation_md: The LCR is intended to provide enough cash to cover funding needs over a 30-day period of stress.

payload.stem_md: Under the Reserve Bank's 2025 Capital Adequacy Directions, what is the minimum CET1 ratio, excluding the capital conservation buffer?
payload.correct_explanation_md: CET1 capital shall be at least 5.5 per cent of RWAs on an ongoing basis.

payload.stem_md: What is the minimum total capital ratio including the capital conservation buffer under the Directions?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The minimum total capital ratio plus CCB is 9 + 2.5 = 11.5 per cent.

payload.stem_md: Within the 7 per cent minimum Tier 1 ratio, what is the most that Additional Tier 1 can count for?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Within the minimum Tier 1 capital, AT1 capital can be admitted at a maximum of 1.5 per cent of RWAs.

payload.stem_md: A wholly owned subsidiary of a foreign bank in India begins operations. What minimum capital adequacy ratio applies for the first three years?

options.text_md: 10 per cent, plus the capital conservation buffer and other buffers

payload.correct_explanation_md: A WOS must maintain a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 10 per cent for an initial three years, plus the CCB and other buffers.

payload.stem_md: Under the Basic Indicator Approach, operational risk capital is based on:

options.text_md: The average over three years of 15 per cent of positive annual gross income
A fixed 8 per cent of loans

payload.correct_explanation_md: Capital equals the average over the previous three years of alpha (15 per cent) times positive annual gross income.

payload.stem_md: How are risk weighted assets for market risk obtained from the market risk capital charge?
payload.correct_explanation_md: RWAs for market risk are the market risk capital charge multiplied by 12.5.

payload.stem_md: Which three risk classes make up the market risk capital charge under the Directions?

options.text_md: Basis, yield curve and option risk
Interest rate risk, equity risk and foreign exchange risk

payload.correct_explanation_md: The market risk capital charge is the sum of capital requirements for interest rate risk, equity risk and foreign exchange risk.

payload.stem_md: A bank has risk-weighted assets of ₹18,400 crore. What is the minimum total capital including the capital conservation buffer, in ₹ crore?
A bank has risk-weighted assets of ₹12,500 crore. What minimum CET1 capital must it hold including the capital conservation buffer, in ₹ crore?
payload.correct_explanation_md: CET1 minimum 5.5% plus buffer 2.5% = 8%. 8% of 12,500 = 1,000.

payload.stem_md: Until 30 September 2021 a bank had to hold total capital of 10.875% of risk-weighted assets. On risk-weighted assets of ₹20,000 crore, how much more capital was needed from 1 October 2021 under the full 11.5%, in ₹ crore?

unresolved: The Basel Committee texts (Basel I, the 1996 amendment, Basel II, Basel III) were not read; their content is the courseware's account, which agrees with the standard text on the points taught (8 per cent, risk weights, VaR parameters, pillars). The courseware states that the capital conservation buffer was fully effective by 1 October 2021; that is the Indian date and is taught as such, not as the BCBS timetable (the BCBS buffer was phased from 2016 to 2019).

The Directions copy used is updated to 7 October 2026, after the cut-off; paragraphs 7, 11, 182-185, 214-215 and Table 1 were used and later amendments were not compared. The courseware's statements about the 2007 roadmap, the 5 February 2021 circular and the 1 April 2013 start were not checked against the original circulars.
The courseware lists the BCBS groups, G20 details and FSB principles; these are not taught as exam facts.

Leverage ratio, countercyclical buffer, D-SIB, credit risk weights, credit risk mitigation, market risk and operational risk charges, Pillar 2 and 3 detail and risk based supervision (courseware sections 13.8 to 13.18) are covered in the following batches.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.

items.title: Why Basel I was revised, and Basel II's three pillars
items.core_explanation_md:
**Basel I's weaknesses**: weights **not risk-sensitive** (all corporates at 100%, **AAA same as B**; all banks at 20%); **regulation-driven decisions** rather than economic ones; **no credit for mitigants** (derivatives, securitisation, collateral, guarantees); **no operational risk**.

**Basel II** (**June 2004**, comprehensive version **June 2006**)
| Pillar | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **1 Minimum capital** | credit, market and **new** operational risk |
| **2 Supervisory review** | assess risk, **soundness of internal processes**, **minimum capital with prompt corrective action**, **extra capital** where processes are weak |
| **3 Market discipline** | **enhanced disclosure** (core and supplementary, timely) |

items.title: The Pillar 1 menu of approaches
items.core_explanation_md:
| Risk | Approaches, **simplest to most advanced** |
| --- | --- |
| **Credit** | **Standardised**; **Foundation IRB**; **Advanced IRB** |
| **Market** | **Standardised** (**maturity method** or **duration method**); **internal models** |
| **Operational** | **Basic Indicator**; **Standardised**; **Advanced Measurement** |

More advanced approaches are **more risk-sensitive** and need **supervisory approval**.

items.title: Basel III: why, and what it added
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why**: the **2008 crisis** exposed **too much leverage**, **thin liquidity buffers**, **weak governance and incentives**. BCBS issued **liquidity principles (September 2008)** and **Basel III (December 2010)**, endorsed by the **G20 at Seoul (November 2010)**.

**Innovations**
- **Better and more capital**: BCBS minimum **common equity 4.5%** and **Tier 1 6%** from **2015**.
- **Capital conservation buffer**: **common equity**; if breached, **pay-outs are restricted**.
- **Countercyclical buffer**: curbs **bank participation in system-wide credit booms**.
- **Leverage ratio**: **backstop** to risk-based capital.
- **LCR**: **30 days of stress**, **60% in 2015 to 100% in 2019**.
- **NSFR**: **minimum standard from 1 January 2018** (longer-term funding mismatch).
- **Systemically important banks**: **extra requirements**.

**Three pillars kept**, each **enhanced**.

items.title: Indian minimum capital ratios under Basel III
items.core_explanation_md:
| Item | % of risk-weighted assets |
| --- | --- |
| **Minimum CET1** | **5.5** |
| **Minimum Tier 1** | **7.0** (so **AT1 at most 1.5**) |
| **Minimum total capital (CRAR)** | **9.0** (so **Tier 2 at most 2.0**) |
| **Capital conservation buffer (CET1)** | **2.5** |
| **CET1 + buffer** | **8.0** |
| **Total capital + buffer** | **11.5** |

- **Foreign bank wholly owned subsidiary**: **10%** minimum for the **first three years**, plus buffers.
- **Levels**: **solo** and **consolidated**; **insurance and non-financial subsidiaries are not consolidated**.
- **Phasing (courseware)**: from **1 April 2013**; the **last 0.625% of the buffer** was **deferred to 1 October 2021**, so until **30 September 2021** buffer **1.875%** and CRAR **10.875%**; from **1 October 2021** **2.5%** and **11.5%**.

items.title: How the Directions build capital for operational and market risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Operational risk: Basic Indicator Approach**: capital = **average over the previous three years of 15% (alpha) of positive annual gross income**; **years with zero or negative gross income are left out** of both numerator and denominator.

**Market risk**: charge = **interest rate risk + equity risk + foreign exchange risk**; **risk weighted assets for market risk = charge × 12.5**.

**History (courseware)**: in **2007** the Reserve Bank asked banks to adopt the **standardised approach** (credit), **Basic Indicator** (operational, by **March 2009**) and the **standardised duration approach** (market); **advanced approaches** need **prior RBI approval**.

items.title: The capital charge for market risk under the 1996 amendment
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank using its own model has a previous day's ten-day VaR of ₹12 crore and an average daily VaR over the preceding 60 business days of ₹9 crore, with the multiplier at 3. What is the market risk capital charge, and what if the previous day's VaR had been ₹30 crore?

worked_steps.description: Compare with the previous day's VaR of 12.
If the previous day's VaR were ₹30 crore.

items.final_answer_with_unit: The charge is ₹27 crore; it would be ₹30 crore if the previous day's VaR were ₹30 crore

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the charge the higher of the two figures?
self_check.expected_takeaway: So that a sudden rise in risk (a high previous day VaR) is capitalised at once, while the multiple of the 60-day average guards against understating risk in calm periods.

items.title: Risk-weighted assets and the capital ratio under Basel I weights
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank holds government securities of ₹200 crore (0% weight), claims on banks of ₹300 crore (20%), residential mortgage loans of ₹400 crore (50%) and corporate loans of ₹500 crore (100%). Find its risk-weighted assets, the capital needed at 8% and at 9%, and its ratio if it holds capital of ₹95 crore.
items.final_answer_with_unit: Risk-weighted assets are ₹760 crore; capital needed is ₹60.8 crore at 8% and ₹68.4 crore at 9%; a bank with ₹95 crore has a 12.5% ratio

self_check.prompt_text: Why do the government securities add nothing to the risk-weighted assets?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They carry a 0% risk weight, so they need no capital for credit risk.
